newsitem.title: UK: UK papers tighten rules on paying trial witnesses.
newsitem.headline: UK papers tighten rules on paying trial witnesses.

text.p: British newspapers acted on Thursday to head off a legal ban on "chequebook journalism" payments to trial witnesses by strengthening voluntary rules against them.
The government expressed concern last week that payments to trial witnesses could lead to abuses of justice and invited views by the end of the year on a proposal to ban them.
Newspapers and television stations set alarm bells ringing by paying 19 witnesses sums of up to 20,000 pounds ($30,000) before last year's "House of Horrors" trial of serial killer Rosemary West.
But the Press Complaints Commission chairman, Lord John Wakeham, said a tightening of the newspaper industry's voluntary code of practice, published on Thursday, made legislation unnecessary.
"The case for statutory control over self-regulation is not made out at the present time," Wakeham, a former Conservative cabinet minister, told parliament's National Heritage Committee.
Under the new stricter code, editors should make payments only if there is an "overriding need" to do so and must be able to demonstrate that a legitimate public interest is at stake.
To increase transparency, editors must also disclose payments to prosecution and defence lawyers.

"This is, I believe, a significant strengthening of self-regulation in this area -- although it may, of course, be some time before we see what practical impact it has," Wakeham said in a written submission to the committee.
